To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The proof-scheduling technique of [13] can be applied to the multi-party case, and that (2) the proof-scheduling technique can be combined with non-black-box simulation to yield a round-optimal protocol.
(i) the O(n) round protocols of [1, 4, 5] are optimal in the presence of an honest majority and (ii) the O(1) protocols of [1] are optimal when a dishonest majority is present.
- We give the first O(1) -round multi-party protocol with a majority of dishonest parties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Can multi-party computation with a majority of malicious parties be performed in constant rounds?
the following question: What is the round complexity of MPC with a static adversary when a broadcast channel is present?
the following question: What is the round complexity of secure multi-party computation in a model where the majority of the parties can be arbitrarily malicious?

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the first protocol is the first protocol that is secure against a dishonest majority and requires only polylogarithmic communication and rounds, and the second is the first constant round protocol secure in the presence of dishonest majority.
we have shown that, in the presence of an adaptive adversary, the round complexity of secure computation with a broadcast channel can be improved from O(n) to O(log n) or O(1) rounds.
we have shown that the round complexity of MPC is not O(n) in the presence of an adversary who controls a static majority.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the round complexity of secure computation in the presence a dishonest majority is not as large as previously thought.
the round complexity of this setting is not necessarily n.
round complexity is not a barrier to secure computation in the presence a static adversary.
